 What is a “Google Preferred Source”?
 Daylight saving time ends this Sunday, November 1, bringing an extra hour on the clock and earlier sunsets across the Tennessee Valley and surrounding higher elevations.
 At 2:00am on Sunday, clocks will move back one hour to 1:00am. That means the 1:00am hour happens twice. Most smartphones and internet-connected devices should update automatically, but it is a good idea to check clocks that manually need to be changed.
 What does this mean for our region?
 The trade-off is less daylight in the evening. Sunset will arrive earlier, and many people will notice it getting dark before or during the evening commute.
 This change affects communities throughout our region, including the higher elevations. Mountain terrain can also affect when sunlight reaches certain valleys and slopes, so some locations may feel like they lose daylight sooner than others.
 And while we gain an extra hour on the clock, that doesn't mean we're gaining an hour of sunshine. We're simply shifting the timing of daylight.
 Why are the days getting shorter?
 The clock change is not what causes our days to get shorter. That comes down to Earth's tilt.
 Earth is tilted about 23.5 degrees on its axis as it travels around the sun. During fall and winter in the Northern Hemisphere, our part of the planet gradually tilts farther away from the sun.
 As a result, the sun follows a lower and shorter path across the sky. We have fewer hours of daylight, and the sun's angle is lower. This means less direct solar energy reaches the ground.
 The shortest day of the year arrives with the winter solstice on December 21. After that, daylight gradually increases again as we head toward spring.
 Why do we change the clocks?
 Daylight saving time shifts an hour of daylight from the morning to the evening during the warmer months. When we return to standard time in November, that hour shifts back toward the morning.
 The United States first adopted daylight saving time nationally in 1918. The Uniform Time Act of 1966 later established a more consistent schedule for when most of the country changes its clocks.
 After Sunday's change, we will stay on standard time until daylight saving time returns on March 14, 2027.
 A few things to keep in mind
 With sunset arriving earlier, remember that evening commutes and outdoor activities may take place in lower-light conditions. Give yourself extra time on the roads, watch for pedestrians and cyclists, and use appropriate lighting when walking or exercising after dark.
 The fall time change can also affect sleep routines, even though we gain an hour. Keeping a consistent bedtime and wake-up schedule can help make the transition easier.
 So enjoy that extra hour this weekend! Just remember: the clocks are changing, but the shorter days are part of the natural seasonal shift as we move closer to winter.
